title: Classification and Dichotomous Keys
seo_title: Year 7 Science: Classification and Dichotomous Keys Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Investigate the role of classification in ordering and organising the diversity of life on Earth and use and develop dichotomous keys to classify living things (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 7 science worksheets on classification and dichotomous keys: vertebrate and invertebrate groups, monotremes, marsupials and placental mammals, scientific names and using keys. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Group living things by shared features.
key_sub: A dichotomous key uses yes/no questions about observable features.
body_html:
How to think about it

Scientists classify living things into groups by the features they share.

  • Vertebrates (backbone): fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals. Invertebrates: insects, arachnids, crustaceans, molluscs, worms.
  • Australian mammals include monotremes (lay eggs), marsupials (pouch) and placental mammals.
  • A dichotomous key asks pairs of questions about clear, observable features until only one organism is left.
Example

Eight legs, two body parts. Group?

insects have six legs

Answer: arachnid

Example

A koala: which mammal group?

the young grow in a pouch

Answer: marsupial

Common mistakes

  • Classifying by habitat or size instead of body features.
  • Calling spiders insects.
  • Writing key questions that are opinions, such as 'Is it pretty?'

faq.a: Monotremes are mammals that lay eggs. The platypus and the echidnas are the only living monotremes, found in Australia and New Guinea.

faq.q: How do I write a good dichotomous key?
faq.a: Use questions with only two answers about features anyone can see or measure, such as 'Does it have legs?' Split the group at each step until each organism is on its own.

faq.q: Why do species have scientific names?
faq.a: A two-part scientific name, such as Phascolarctos cinereus for the koala, is the same in every country, so scientists know exactly which species they mean.

items.q: Which three broad groups are living things often sorted into?
items.e: Micro-organisms are a third big group.

items.q: Why do scientists use two-part Latin names?
c: Every scientist in the world can use the same name for a species.
items.e: Common names differ from place to place.

items.q: How does a pine tree reproduce?
items.e: Conifers such as pines and firs make seeds in cones.

items.q: What is a dichotomous key?
c: a key with pairs of choices at each step that lead to the name of an organism
a key that opens a cage
a list of animals in alphabetical order
items.e: Dichotomous means dividing into two.

items.q: Is a butterfly a vertebrate or an invertebrate?
items.e: Vertebrates have a backbone; invertebrates do not. A butterfly is an insect.

items.q: In a key, what should each question do?
c: split the group into two smaller groups
items.e: Each question narrows the choices.

items.q: Which is a feature of reptiles such as goannas?
items.e: Reptiles lay eggs with leathery shells on land.

items.q: A platypus has fur, lays eggs and feeds its young milk. Which group is it in?
items.e: Fur and milk make it a mammal.

items.q: Which body part do all fish use to breathe?
items.e: Gills take oxygen from water.

items.q: Why do scientists use keys?
c: to identify living things they do not know quickly and reliably
to give animals names they like
items.e: Keys work in the field.

items.q: Is a seahorse a vertebrate or an invertebrate?
items.e: Vertebrates have a backbone; invertebrates do not. Seahorses have gills and fins: fish.

items.q: Is a squid a vertebrate or an invertebrate?
items.e: Vertebrates have a backbone; invertebrates do not. A squid has a soft body: a mollusc.

items.q: Is a shark a vertebrate or an invertebrate?
items.e: Vertebrates have a backbone; invertebrates do not. A shark is a fish.

items.q: How do you tell an insect from an arachnid?
c: Insects have six legs; arachnids have eight.
Insects have eight legs; arachnids have six.
items.e: Count the legs.

items.q: What does classifying living things mean?
c: giving every animal a pet name
putting them in order of size
sorting them into groups by what they have in common
items.e: Scientists sort by observable characteristics.

items.q: Why do scientists classify living things?
c: to organise them into groups by shared features so they are easier to study
to sort them by size only
to decide which ones are pretty
items.e: Classification shows relationships.

items.q: What is a vertebrate?
c: an animal that lives in water
items.e: Vertebrates have a spine.

items.q: How does a fir tree reproduce?
items.e: Conifers such as pines and firs make seeds in cones.

items.q: Which group do frogs belong to?
items.e: Amphibians usually live in water when young and on land as adults.

items.q: You reach the end of a branch in a key. What is there?
c: the name of one living thing
a list of all the animals
items.e: Each branch ends with one name.

items.q: Which group does an octopus belong to?
items.e: An octopus has a soft body: a mollusc.

items.q: An animal breathes with lungs and gives birth to live young that drink milk. Which group does it belong to?
items.e: This is a key characteristic of mammals.

items.q: Which group does a seahorse belong to?
items.e: Seahorses have gills and fins: fish.

items.q: An animal has a soft body and moves on a muscular foot. Which group does it belong to?
items.e: This is a key characteristic of molluscs.

items.q: Which of these animals is a bird?
items.e: An eagle is a bird.

items.q: Which animal does NOT belong with the others: crab, salmon, shrimp, slater?
items.e: The other three are crustaceans; a salmon is a fish.

items.q: Which of these animals is an arachnid?
items.e: Ticks have 8 legs: arachnids.

items.q: Which group does a squid belong to?
items.e: A squid has a soft body: a mollusc.

items.q: Which group does a shrimp belong to?
items.e: A shrimp is a crustacean.

items.q: Which animal does NOT belong with the others: barnacle, beetle, lobster, shrimp?
items.e: The other three are crustaceans; a beetle is one of the insects.

items.q: An animal has a hard outer shell and many jointed legs, and most live in water. Which group does it belong to?
items.e: This is a key characteristic of crustaceans.

items.q: Which animal does NOT belong with the others: fox, possum, whale, slater?
items.e: The other three are mammals; a slater is one of the crustaceans.

items.q: Which group does a snake belong to?
items.e: A snake is a reptile.

items.q: Which of these animals is a fish?
items.e: A goldfish is a fish.

items.q: An animal starts life in water as a tadpole-like larva and later lives on land. Which group does it belong to?
items.e: This is a key characteristic of amphibians.

items.q: Which group does a crocodile belong to?
items.e: A crocodile is a reptile.

items.q: An animal has feathers, a beak and lays eggs with hard shells. Which group does it belong to?
items.e: This is a key characteristic of birds.

items.q: Which of these animals is a mammal?
items.e: Dolphins breathe air and feed their young on milk: mammals.

items.q: Which of these animals is a reptile?
items.e: A gecko is a reptile.

items.q: Which animal does NOT belong with the others: crocodile, gecko, lizard, tick?
items.e: The other three are reptiles; a tick is one of the arachnids.

items.q: Which group of mammals does the hopping mouse belong to?
items.e: A placental mammal is a mammal whose young grow inside the mother, fed by a placenta.

items.q: Which of these animals is a mammal whose young grow inside the mother, fed by a placenta?
items.e: The flying fox is a placental mammal.

items.q: Which group of mammals does the short-beaked echidna belong to?
items.e: A monotreme is a mammal that lays eggs.

items.q: Is a fir tree a flowering or a non-flowering plant?
items.e: A fir tree does not make flowers. It reproduces with seeds in cones.

items.q: Which group of mammals does the flying fox belong to?
items.e: A placental mammal is a mammal whose young grow inside the mother, fed by a placenta.

items.q: Which group of mammals does the koala belong to?
items.e: A marsupial is a mammal whose young grow in a pouch.

items.q: Is a fern a flowering or a non-flowering plant?
items.e: A fern does not make flowers. It reproduces with spores.

items.q: Which is the best question for a dichotomous key?
items.e: Key questions must be about features anyone can observe.

items.q: Why is a spider not an insect?
c: It has eight legs and two body parts; insects have six legs and three body parts.
items.e: Spiders are arachnids.

items.q: Which group of mammals does the dugong belong to?
items.e: A placental mammal is a mammal whose young grow inside the mother, fed by a placenta.

items.q: Is a daisy a flowering or a non-flowering plant?
items.e: A daisy makes flowers and seeds.

items.q: Which of these animals is a mammal whose young grow inside the mother, fed by a placenta?
items.e: The dugong is a placental mammal.

items.q: What is the scientific name of the koala?
items.e: Scientific names have two parts: genus and species.

items.q: Is a moss a flowering or a non-flowering plant?
items.e: A moss does not make flowers. It reproduces with spores.

items.q: How does a moss reproduce?
items.e: Ferns, mosses, liverworts and horsetails make tiny spores.

items.q: Which group of mammals does the platypus belong to?
items.e: A monotreme is a mammal that lays eggs.

items.q: Is a dandelion a flowering or a non-flowering plant?
items.e: A dandelion makes flowers and seeds.

items.q: Which of these animals is a mammal whose young grow in a pouch?
items.e: The koala is a marsupial.

items.q: Is a grass a flowering or a non-flowering plant?
items.e: A grass makes flowers and seeds (grass and wheat have small green flowers).

items.q: Which group of mammals does the sugar glider belong to?
items.e: A marsupial is a mammal whose young grow in a pouch.

items.q: Which question could you use in a key to separate a lizard from a frog?
c: Is it nice to look at?
Does it live mostly in water?
items.e: A good key question has a clear yes or no answer that is different for the two animals.

items.q: Why might two scientists classify the same plant differently at first?
c: They might choose different characteristics to group by.
items.e: Classification is based on chosen features.

items.q: Why might scientists change the classification of an animal?
c: New evidence, such as DNA, shows it is more closely related to another group.
items.e: Science changes with new evidence.

items.q: A newly found animal has fur, breathes air and feeds its young milk, but lives in the sea. How should it be classified?
items.e: Classify by characteristics, not by where it lives.

items.q: Which of these animals is a mammal whose young grow inside the mother, fed by a placenta?
items.e: The hopping mouse is a placental mammal.

items.q: Two animals reach the same end of a key. What does this show?
c: The key needs another question to separate them.
items.e: Improve the key.

items.q: Ruby's key question is 'Is it large?' What is the problem?
c: Large is not clear; people may answer differently.
items.e: Use measurable features, such as 'Is it longer than 10 cm?'

items.q: A newly found animal has feathers and lays eggs. Which group should it be placed in?
items.e: Feathers are only found in birds.

items.q: How could you improve the question 'Does it have lots of legs?'
c: Change it to 'Does it have more than six legs?'

items.e: Make it precise.

items.q: Which of these animals is a mammal that lays eggs?
items.e: The short-beaked echidna is a monotreme.

items.q: Why do scientists use characteristics rather than habitat to classify animals?
c: Animals in the same habitat can be very different, such as a shark and a whale.
items.e: Shared features show relationships.

items.q: Mei's key asks 'Is it big?' Why is this a poor question?
c: Big is not exact, so different people may answer differently.
items.e: Use measurable features.

items.q: Which feature do all vertebrates share?
items.e: Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals are vertebrates.

items.q: Which question could you use in a key to separate a snail from a bee?

Is it nice to look at?
items.e: A good key question has a clear yes or no answer that is different for the two animals.

items.q: Which group of mammals does the Tasmanian devil belong to?
items.e: A marsupial is a mammal whose young grow in a pouch.

items.q: Which group of mammals does the common wombat belong to?
items.e: A marsupial is a mammal whose young grow in a pouch.

items.q: Which question would sort a bee from a spider?
items.e: Choose a feature that only one has.

items.q: Mia's key starts 'Does it live in water?' Why is this a weak first question?
c: Habitat is not a body feature; very different animals live in water.
items.e: Use features of the organism.
